title: Pool Fouls Explained: Common Fouls and Ball in Hand for Beginners
description: Learn the most common pool fouls, from scratches to wrong-ball-first, what ball in hand means, and simple habits to avoid giving your opponent a free shot.
body:
Ever watched a pro pool match and heard the crowd groan, then cheer, as the referee waves a hand and the other player gets to put the cue ball anywhere? That is a foul at work. Fouls decide more games than most beginners realise, and with the Mosconi Cup arriving in Orlando on November 27-30, plenty of new fans will be hearing the word all weekend. Here is a friendly guide to the most common pool fouls and what happens next.

What is a foul in pool?

A foul is a rule break during your turn. When you foul, your turn ends and your opponent usually receives ball in hand, which means they can pick up the cue ball and place it wherever they like before shooting. In many rule sets, including the standard World Pool-Billiard Association (WPA) style rules used by the pros, the cue ball can go anywhere on the table.

That is a huge reward, so avoiding fouls is one of the quickest ways to win more games without learning a single new shot.

The most common fouls

1. Scratching the cue ball

If the cue ball drops into a pocket, that is a scratch, and it counts as a foul. It is the one everybody has seen, usually followed by a sigh. Watch your cue ball speed on shots near the pockets, especially when using draw or follow.

2. Hitting the wrong ball first

In 9-ball, your cue ball must touch the lowest-numbered ball on the table first. In 8-ball, once groups are decided, you must contact one of your own balls first. Hitting something else first is a foul even if you pocket a ball by accident.

3. No ball reaches a rail

After the cue ball hits the first object ball, something must either be pocketed or touch a cushion. If nothing does, it is a foul. Beginners meet this one when they play a very soft safety and the balls just kiss and stop.

4. Knocking a ball off the table

A jumped ball is a foul in most rule sets. If it happens on the 8 ball in an 8-ball game, it can cost you the game, so keep an eye on your speed on the break and on power shots.

5. Touching a ball with your hand, clothes or cue

Accidentally nudging a ball with your sleeve, chalk or cue tip is a foul. Take your time leaning over the table and keep your bridge hand steady and clear of other balls.

6. Double hits and pushes

If the cue tip touches the cue ball twice on one stroke, that is a double hit. When the cue ball is very close to the object ball, take extra care to follow through straight and smoothly. A push shot, where the tip stays on the cue ball while it contacts the object ball, is also illegal in standard rules.

7. Both feet off the floor

Under WPA-style rules, at least one foot must touch the floor when you shoot. It sounds silly until you see someone lean far over a table to reach a long shot. Keep a foot planted, or use the rest (mechanical bridge).

Fouls in 8-ball vs 9-ball

The big idea is the same in both games, but a couple of details are different. In 8-ball, pocketing the 8 ball on the same shot as a foul is typically a loss of game. In 9-ball, if the 9 ball drops during a foul it is usually brought back to the table (respotted) instead, and your opponent still gets ball in hand. Not sure how the two games compare? Our 8-ball vs 9-ball vs 10-ball guide breaks it down, and the 9-ball rules explainer covers the push-out and the break.

Call the foul, then keep playing

In casual play, fouls are usually called by the opponent. A common rule is that a foul must be called before the next shot is taken, so speak up politely and promptly. In league and tournament play, a referee or captain may handle it. Whatever the setting, stay friendly: most fouls are honest mistakes, and good sportsmanship matters as much as good shooting. Our pool etiquette guide has more.

A quick rule check: house rules vary

Bar tables, leagues and pro events do not always use the same rulebook. Some leagues limit where you can place the cue ball after a foul, and some treat a break foul differently. Before you play for fun or for a prize, ask what rules are in use. It takes ten seconds and avoids arguments.

How to avoid fouls: a short checklist

  • Pick the legal target ball before you bend down.
  • Check where the cue ball could travel after contact.
  • Keep one foot on the floor and your clothing clear of the balls.
  • Use a smooth, straight follow-through when the balls are close together.
  • Follow a steady pre-shot routine so you do not rush.

Watch fouls (and great shots) live

The best way to see the rules in action is to watch the pros, and the Mosconi Cup is the perfect stage. Check our Mosconi Cup 2026 hub for the weekend, or look at the this weekend page for events near you.

So what is the foul you see most at your table? Pick one from the list, watch for it in your next game, and you will be surprised how many you can dodge.
